title: Civil Rights in depth
examples: What were some of the key laws passed during the Civil Rights Movement?
How did different leaders use different methods to achieve change?
Can you compare the strategies used in the US and India's independence movements?

explain.say: Today we explore the Civil Rights Movement in depth. We will look at different strategies used for change.

items: Protests and marches showed public support.
Boycotts stopped economic activity for change.
Legal challenges used the court system.

explain.say: Another key strategy was direct action. This meant non-violent resistance to unfair laws. For example, sit-ins were used to challenge segregated lunch counters.
Legislation was a major goal. This meant passing new laws to end unfair practices. A clear example is the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Leaders were crucial figures who guided the movement. Martin Luther King Jr. was a major leader known for his speeches. He inspired many people to act.

draw.text: Key Leader: Martin Luther King Jr.

explain.say: In everyday life, we see this when companies adopt diversity policies. They create rules to ensure all employees are treated fairly.
A common mistake is thinking that only big marches work. Sometimes, smaller, persistent local actions build up the necessary momentum for change.

faq.q: What was the main difference between protest and boycott?
faq.a: A protest is a public demonstration to show disagreement. A boycott is a refusal to buy or use goods or services to pressure for change.
asks: What is the difference between protesting and picketing?
Can a boycott be used without a formal protest?

faq.q: Why was passing new legislation so important?
faq.a: Legislation made the changes official and legally binding for everyone. It provided a lasting structure for equality.
asks: Does a law make something right forever?
What is the legal power behind civil rights?

faq.q: Were all leaders in the movement the same?
faq.a: No, there were many leaders with different backgrounds and approaches. Some focused on legal battles while others focused on direct action.
asks: Did everyone agree on the methods used?
Who were the main figures of the movement?

faq.q: Did the movement happen all at once?
faq.a: No, it was a long process spanning many years. Change often builds slowly through many small victories.
asks: Was the movement quick or slow?
What was the timeline of the struggle?

faq.q: What does 'non-violence' mean in this context?
faq.a: It means opposing injustice without using physical violence against people or property. It relies on moral strength.
asks: What is the power of peaceful resistance?

facts: The movement used both legal action and public protest.
Boycotts aimed to create economic pressure on segregation.
Legislation provided the necessary legal enforcement for rights.
Non-violent resistance was a core tactic taught by many leaders.

quiz.say: Which action involves refusing to use services to create economic pressure?
quiz.why: A boycott is specifically the refusal to use or buy something to force a change.

wrong.1: Protests are public demonstrations, not necessarily economic refusals.
wrong.2: Legislation is the written law itself, not the action taken.
wrong.3: Direct action is a broad term; boycott is a specific type of action.

quiz.say: If a group successfully passes a major anti-discrimination law, what did they achieve?
quiz.why: Legislation refers to the creation of official, written laws that enforce rights.

wrong.0: Protests raise awareness, but legislation makes the change official.
wrong.1: Direct action is the method used to push for the law to be written.
wrong.3: A boycott is a tactic used to achieve legislation, not the law itself.

quiz.say: A leader known for speeches urging non-violent resistance was:
quiz.why: Martin Luther King Jr. is historically recognized for his role and speeches in the movement.

wrong.0: John Lewis was a key activist, but King is often cited for the unifying speeches.
wrong.2: Rosa Parks was crucial for her direct action, but King is noted for his broader leadership speeches.
wrong.3: Malcolm X advocated for different, more militant approaches at times.
